blind_target.title: Do Get-Out-the-Vote Calls Reduce Turnout? The Importance of Statistical Methods for Field Experiments.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Replication of Professor Imai’s (2005) analysis reveals a series of errors that call into question the magnitude, significance, and robustness of his matching estimates.
blind_target.outcome_computational_quote: Table 9 of Imai 2005 exaggerates the significance of the phone effect by reporting a coefficient of 6.5 with a standard error of 3.2. These numbers imply a t-ratio of 2.03, which tells the reader at a glance that the effect is statistically significant using a two-sided test (p < .05). When these numbers are replicated using 500,000 bootstrap samples rather than 500, the correct estimate is 6.2, with a t-ratio of 1.87 (see Table 2).
blind_target.outcome_robustness_quote: The estimated effects of phone calls fall to insignificance when based on the actual sample. His matching program generates an estimate of 5.1 (SE = 3.3) when performing one-to-five matching on the actual sample, and this number drops to 3.6 (SE = 4.5) when one-to-five matching is performed with replacement.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Re-running the original matching analysis yields substantive numerical discrepancies and inflated reported significance. Alternative matching specifications and analysis of actual rather than bootstrap samples remove significance. This target is itself an earlier reanalysis, directly re-tested here.

prior_decision.reason: Omitted target: Under the codebook rules for replication chains and earlier replication/reanalysis attempts, an earlier reanalysis is a target when the current paper directly re-tests its findings. Gerber and Green (2005) directly re-runs Imai (2005)'s propensity score matching code and analysis on the dataset Imai analyzed (Table 2, pp. 308-310), demonstrating computational discrepancies and robustness failures, and also tests Imai's 6.5 percentage point estimate in the 2002 replication experiment.
